doc.title: Jim Cullum interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Teaching combos versus big bands at Stanford
summary: Rowe notes schools favor big bands; Cullum says every Stanford student played in a combo and had to solo.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: You know from teaching jazz in a performance manner, one thing I think may be an issue is that schools are about numbers often times. And the best way to get a lot of kids involved in jazz is to have a big band. And also from a teacher’s standpoint who may not know that much about jazz, they can handle a big band sort of because they’ve got all this music. So they can have a big band, but to have a combo, that’s a different story. First of all you don’t have as many kids that are going to be involved, and you really have to know a lot more I think, to instruct a combo. So I think that’s one thing that makes it harder to teach small group jazz.
We did it at Stanford and every kid that went to Stanford would be part of a combo. Some of the combos were bebop oriented combos but they were still combos.

Every single kid was part of a combo. And the combos were all a maximum of about seven pieces. And every kid would have to play some solos. I mean they might have a hard time playing solos but in other words you couldn’t just be buried in a section. So, and we need to get, I mean if all you do is just read the music it becomes harder to infuse it with jazz feeling. It’s just harder. It can be done of course.
